meta.title: Who really said "Imagination rules the world"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Documented — but as a memoir, not Napoleon’s pen: Las Cases records him saying ‘l’imagination gouverne le monde’ on Saint Helena, January 1816.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Imagination rules the world'?
meta.ogDescription: Napoleon is recorded saying it on Saint Helena in January 1816 — but only in Las Cases’s memoir of 1823, and in French.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1769–1821 · Emperor of the French, exiled on Saint Helena
answer.sourceLine: The line is documented, but not in anything Napoleon wrote. His companion Emmanuel de Las Cases recorded him saying it at Longwood on Saint Helena in January 1816, and published the exchange in the Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène in 1823, after Napoleon’s death — in French, as “Oui, l’imagination gouverne le monde!” The famous five English words are that book’s 1823 translator’s rendering ↗, stripped of the sentence before it: “This is fanaticism!”

source.heading: Where the line actually appears

docMeta.dd: Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène, by Emmanuel, comte de Las Cases
At Longwood, Saint Helena, January 1816 — dated 7 January 1816 by researcher Shannon Selin
1823, in French (London: Henri Colburn), after Napoleon’s death
“Imagination rules the world” renders “l’imagination gouverne le monde” in the 1823 English edition (Lexington, KY: Thomas Smith)

source.excerpt: The Emperor could not refrain from evincing some emotion at these two circumstances; so strongly did the countenances, accents, and gestures of these two men bear the stamp of truth. He then said, “See the effect of imagination? How powerful is its influence! Here are people who do not know me—who have never seen me; they have only heard me spoken of; and what do they not feel! what would they not do to serve me! And the same caprice is to be found in all countries, in all ages, and in both sexes! This is fanaticism! Yes, imagination rules the world!”
trail: 1815 — Hugh Henry Brackenridge’s novel Modern Chivalry already prints the English sentence “imagination governs the world,” a year before the Saint Helena conversation, as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

January 1816 — At Longwood, Las Cases records Napoleon’s reaction to sailors who wept at the sight of him: “This is fanaticism! Yes, imagination rules the world!” Napoleonic researcher Shannon Selin dates the exchange to 7 January 1816 ↗.

1823 — The Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène is published after Napoleon’s death and becomes a bestseller; the French text reads “Oui, l’imagination gouverne le monde!” ↗ and an English edition appears the same year.

1927 — The New Dictionary of Thoughts prints the bare five-word form, “Imagination rules the world.—Napoleon,” per Quote Investigator ↗ — the sentence is now fully detached from the sailors, the fanaticism and the source.
source.excerptNote: From the 1823 English translation of the Mémorial. The two “circumstances” are British sailors who had never met Napoleon and went to some risk simply to look at him. The popular quotation keeps only the last five words.

author.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
author.heading: About Napoleon Bonaparte
author.bio: Born in Ajaccio, Corsica, on 15 August 1769, Napoleon Bonaparte rose through the armies of the French Revolution to become Emperor of the French in 1804. After Waterloo in June 1815 the British exiled him to Saint Helena in the South Atlantic, where he died at Longwood on 5 May 1821. Almost everything he is quoted as saying in those last years reaches us second-hand, through the notebooks of the companions who shared the exile with him.

cite.sourceCitation: Las Cases, Emmanuel, comte de. Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène: Journal de la vie privée et des conversations de l’empereur Napoléon à Sainte Hélène. Tome I, seconde partie. London: Henri Colburn et Co. and M. Bossange et Co., 1823, 110 (“Voilà le fanatisme! Oui, l’imagination gouverne le monde!”). English translation: Memorial de Sainte Helene: Journal of the Private Life and Conversations of the Emperor Napoleon at Saint Helena. Lexington, KY: Printed by Thomas Smith, 1823 (“This is fanaticism! Yes, imagination rules the world!”).

misattribution.heading: What gets lost between Longwood and the poster
misattribution.intro: Nobody invented this one — but almost nobody quotes it as it stands in the record, and almost nobody names the record.

items.why: Aggregators print the five words under Napoleon’s name with nothing attached. The Goodreads entry, for instance, gives only the author name, no book and no date ↗ — which is why the line is so often assumed to come from something Napoleon wrote.

As recorded, he spoke French: “Oui, l’imagination gouverne le monde!” “Rules” is one English choice among several, and the competing rendering survives in parallel — Wikiquote lists “Imagination governs the world” from Napoleon: In His Own Words (1916) ↗.

The popular form drops the clause immediately before it. In the 1823 text ↗ the full sentence is “This is fanaticism! Yes, imagination rules the world!” — a remark about strangers’ irrational devotion to him, not about creative vision.

Quote Investigator found the English sentence “imagination governs the world” in Brackenridge’s novel Modern Chivalry in 1815 — a year before the Saint Helena conversation. QI notes the coincidence ↗ without claiming Napoleon took the line from there.

A 1980 Dictionary of Foreign Quotations puts a similar saying about imagination in Pascal’s mouth, but Quote Investigator points out that older printings of the Pascal text read “l’opinion,” not “l’imagination” ↗ — an alteration, not a source.

misattribution.truthLine: The best documentary basis is Emmanuel de Las Cases’s Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène (1823) ↗, which records Napoleon at Longwood in January 1816 saying “Voilà le fanatisme! Oui, l’imagination gouverne le monde!” — a companion’s journal, published after his death, not Napoleon’s own pen.

context.heading: What he was actually talking about
lead: In the first days of January 1816, on Saint Helena, Las Cases watched two British sailors go out of their way to get a look at the deposed Emperor. One slipped past the sentries into the garden at Longwood, said he would now die content, and prayed for Napoleon’s health. Another appeared at the gate at Briars with a nosegay of wild flowers, wept, made a clumsy bow, and vanished without handing it over.

Napoleon was visibly moved — and then turned the moment into an observation about himself. These were men who had never met him and knew him only by report, yet would do anything for him. That, he said, is what fanaticism is; and it is imagination, not knowledge, that produces it. Lifted out of the paragraph, the five surviving words read like a compliment to creativity. In place, they are a cold remark about the power of a legend over people who have no first-hand information at all — his own included.
context.detailsSummary: How much weight should the Mémorial carry?
detailsBody: The Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène is the single largest source of “Napoleon quotes” in circulation, and it needs handling with care. Las Cases began his journal two days after Waterloo and transcribed the Emperor’s conversation almost daily until the governor expelled him from the island at the end of 1816; his son made fair copies, and Las Cases periodically showed Napoleon excerpts to obtain his approval ↗.

That is closer to a vetted record than most memoirs manage — and also a reason for caution, since the book was published in 1823, after Napoleon’s death, and became one of the founding texts of the Napoleonic legend it describes. A sentence in the Mémorial is good evidence that Napoleon said something like it. It is not the same thing as a manuscript in his hand.
